fixes.explanation: Quarrels don't come up in this verse. Paul's compliment is about two things: they remember him in everything, and they maintain the traditions just as he passed them on. Nothing in his words here says anything about arguments. This is a plain, warm commendation, so take it as one.

Moses was Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), a giant of a name, but Paul never mentions him in this verse. He says, “…the head of every man is Christ…” That's the name that fills the blank. Easy to grab a famous name when you're in a hurry, baker. I've grabbed the wrong cookie cutter in a hurry, too.

Abraham is called Israel's father (Isaiah 51:2), but he's not in this verse at all. Paul says, “…the head of every man is Christ…” So the blank is Christ. Paul names the heads here, and Abraham isn't one of them.

That's what Paul says: “Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head.” He starts with the man, and in the very next verse he turns to the woman. Hold onto that word dishonors, baker, because it comes back.

Humility is a nice word, but it's not Paul's word here. He says, “Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head.” Humility sounds like it would fit, I'll give you that. But dishonors is the word Paul uses.

Elders are a good guess, but this verse never mentions them. Paul says a man who prays or prophesies with his head covered “…dishonors his head.” The one being dishonored is his own head, and nobody else is named.
Yes, this one is false. Paul says a woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered “…dishonors her head…” The word is dishonors, not honors. You read that one carefully, baker.
Lift isn't Paul's word. He says, “…she should cover her head.” A lifted head sounds confident, I'll give you that. But the verse says nothing about lifting anything.
Baptism doesn't come up in this verse. Paul says, “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God…” His reason is about who a man is, not about being first in any line.

Born of the Spirit sounds spiritual, I'll give you that. But Paul is talking about how people come into the world, and he says, “…so also man is born of woman.” He's pointing to birth from a mother, right alongside woman coming from man.
Waiting sounds patient, but Paul hands the question to them right away. Before it he says, “Judge for yourselves…” He puts the weighing in their hands, not on his arrival.

Yes, this one is false. Paul asks if nature teaches that “…if a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him…” The glory belongs to the woman, he says: “…if a woman has long hair, it is her glory?” You saw who gets which, baker.
Reward would be a sweet way to see hair, I'll give you that. But Paul says, “For long hair is given to her as a covering.” That's the word he picks for what it's given as.
